metadata.title: Upper bounds for multicolour Ramsey numbers

nodes.statement: \leavevmode\unskip\nolinebreak\space\textcolor{blue!80!black}{[Theorem 1.1]}\space\ignorespaces For each \(r \geqslant 2\), there exists \(\delta = \delta(r) > 0\) such that \begin{equation*} R_r(k) \leqslant e^{-\delta k} r^{rk} \end{equation*} for all sufficiently large \(k \in \mathbb{N}\).
nodes.label: thm:Ramsey:multicolour

nodes.name: Multinomial coefficient bound
nodes.statement: \leavevmode\unskip\nolinebreak\space\textcolor{blue!80!black}{[Lemma A.1]}\space\ignorespaces For each \(k,t,r \in \mathbb{N}\) with \(3 \leqslant t \leqslant k\), we have \begin{equation*} \binom{rk-t}{k,\dots,k,k-t} \leqslant e^{-(r-1)t^2/3rk} r^{rk-t}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:multibounds

nodes.statement: To prove this, observe that \begin{equation*} \binom{rk-t}{k,\dots,k,k-t} \binom{rk}{k,\dots,k}^{-1} = \, \prod_{i = 0}^{t - 1} \frac{k - i}{rk - i} = r^{-t} \,\prod_{i = 0}^{t-1} \bigg( 1 - \frac{(r-1)i}{rk - i} \bigg) \leqslant r^{-t} \cdot e^{-(r-1)t^2/3rk}. \end{equation*} Since \(\binom{rk}{k,\dots,k} \leqslant r^{rk}\), the claimed bound follows.

nodes.name: Edge colouring
nodes.statement: An edge colouring of a graph \(G\) with colours \(C\) is a map from the edge set \(E(G)\) to \(C\).
nodes.label: def:edge-colouring

nodes.name: Colour neighbourhood
nodes.statement: Given an edge colouring, we write \(N_i(u)\) to denote the neighbourhood of vertex \(u\) in colour \(i\).
nodes.label: def:colour-neighborhood

nodes.name: Function \(p_i(X,Y)\)
nodes.statement: Let \(r, n\in\mathbb{N}\). Given sets \(X,Y \subset V(K_n)\) and a colour \(i \in [r]\), define \begin{equation*} p_i(X,Y) = \min\bigg\{ \frac{|N_i(x) \cap Y|}{|Y|} : x \in X \bigg\}, \end{equation*}
nodes.label: def:p

nodes.name: cosh√x function
nodes.statement: Define \(\cosh \sqrt{x}\) via its Taylor expansion \begin{equation*} \cosh\sqrt{x} = \sum_{n = 0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{(2n)!}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: def:coshsqrt

nodes.name: Bounds on \(\cosh\sqrt{x}\) for positive arguments
nodes.statement: \(x \leqslant 2 + \cosh \sqrt{x} \leqslant 3 e^{\sqrt{x}}\) for every \(x > 0\).
nodes.label: lem:coshsqrt-bd-pos

nodes.statement: For the lower-bound, using the fact that \(x>0\) and all coefficients of \(\cosh \sqrt{x}\) are positive, \begin{equation*} 2+\cosh \sqrt{x} - x \geqslant 2 - \frac{x}{2} + \frac{x^2}{24} = \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{24}(x-6)^2 \geqslant 0. \end{equation*} For the upper bound, we observe that because by comparing coefficients, \begin{equation*} e^{\sqrt{x}} = \sum 3\frac{x^{n/2}}{n!} \geqslant \cosh\sqrt{x} \end{equation*} Finally, \(2e^{\sqrt{x}}\geqslant 2\) when \(x>0\).

nodes.name: Bounds on \(\cosh\sqrt{x}\) for negative arguments
nodes.statement: \(-1 \leqslant \cosh \sqrt{x} \leqslant 1\) for every \(x < 0\).
nodes.label: lem:coshsqrt-bd-neg

nodes.statement: From the Taylor expansion, we get \(\cosh \sqrt{x} = \cos \sqrt{-x}\).

nodes.name: Lower bound for cosh√x
nodes.statement: For all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), it is \(1 \leqslant 2 + \cosh\sqrt{x}\).
nodes.label: lem:le-coshsqrt

nodes.statement: When \(x\) is negative, we use \(\cosh \sqrt{x} = \cos \sqrt{-x}\geqslant -1\). When \(x\) is positive this is implied by the fact that all coefficients in the power series of \(\cosh \sqrt{x}\) are positive.
Let \(r \in \mathbb{N}\). \begin{equation} f(x_1,\dots,x_r) = \sum_{j = 1}^r x_j \prod_{i \ne j} \big( 2 + \cosh\sqrt{x_i} \big). \end{equation}
nodes.label: def:f

nodes.statement: All of the coefficients of the Taylor expansion of \(f\) are non-negative.
nodes.label: lem:taylor-nonneg

nodes.statement: By definition \(2+\cosh\sqrt{x}\) has positive coefficients. It suffices to observe that the product and sum of two Taylor series with only positive coefficients has again positive coefficients. Since \(f\) is such a combination of sums and products of Taylor series with only positive coefficients, we get the claim.

nodes.name: Integration by parts for special functions
nodes.label: lem:integration-by-parts-special

nodes.name: Moments lemma
nodes.statement: \leavevmode\unskip\nolinebreak\space\textcolor{blue!80!black}{[Lemma 3.2]}\space\ignorespaces Let \(U\) and \(U'\) be i.i.d.~random variables taking values in a finite set~\(X\), and let \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r \colon X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^n\) be arbitrary functions. Then \begin{equation*} \mathbb{E}\Big[ \big\langle \sigma_1(U),\sigma_1(U') \big\rangle^{\ell_1} \cdots \big\langle \sigma_r(U),\sigma_r(U') \big\rangle^{\ell_r} \Big] \geqslant 0. \end{equation*} for every \((\ell_1,\dots,\ell_r) \in \mathbb{Z}^r\) with \(\ell_1,\dots,\ell_r \geqslant 0\).
nodes.label: lem:moments

nodes.statement: To simplify the notation, let us write \begin{equation*} \big\langle \sigma_1(U),\sigma_1(U') \big\rangle^{\ell_1} \cdots \big\langle \sigma_r(U), \sigma_r(U') \big\rangle^{\ell_r} = \prod_{i = 1}^\ell \big\langle \sigma_{a_i}(U), \sigma_{a_i}(U') \big\rangle \end{equation*} where \(\ell = \ell_1 + \cdots + \ell_r\) and \((a_1,\dots,a_\ell)\) is such that \(\big| \big\{ i \in [\ell] : a_i = j \big\} \big| = \ell_j\) for each \(j \in [r]\). Now set \begin{equation*} Z = \sigma_{a_1}(U) \otimes \sigma_{a_2}(U) \otimes \cdots \otimes \sigma_{a_\ell}(U) \quad \text{and} \quad Z' = \sigma_{a_1}(U') \otimes \sigma_{a_2}(U') \otimes \cdots \otimes \sigma_{a_\ell}(U'), \end{equation*} and note that \begin{equation*} \big\langle Z, Z' \big\rangle = \prod_{i = 1}^\ell \big\langle \sigma_{a_i}(U), \sigma_{a_i}(U') \big\rangle, \end{equation*} since \(\langle u_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes u_r, v_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes v_r \rangle = \langle u_1, v_1 \rangle \cdots \langle v_r , u_r \rangle \) for any vectors \(u_i,v_i \in \mathbb{R}^n\). Finally, note that \(Z\) and \(Z'\) are independent and identically distributed random vectors, and therefore \begin{equation*} \mathbb{E} \big[ \langle Z, Z' \rangle \big] = \mathbb{E}_{Z'} \big[ \mathbb{E}_Z \big[ \langle Z, Z' \rangle \big] \big] = \mathbb{E}_{Z'} \big[ \big\langle \mathbb{E}[Z], Z' \big\rangle \big] = \big\langle \mathbb{E}[Z], \mathbb{E}[Z'] \big\rangle \geqslant 0, \end{equation*} as required, where the final inequality holds because \(\mathbb{E}[Z] = \mathbb{E}[Z']\).

Let \(g(x):= cosh(\sqrt{x})\) where \(cosh(x)\) is defined by \(cosh(\sqrt{x})=\overunderset{\infty}{n=0}{\sum}\frac{x^n}{(2n)!}\), then: \begin{enumerate} \item For all \(x\geqslant 0\), we have \(x \leqslant 2+cosh(\sqrt{x}) \leqslant 3e^{\sqrt{x}}\). \item For all \(x <0\), we have \(-1 \leqslant cosh(\sqrt{x})\leqslant 1\). In particular, \(2+cosh(x)\geqslant 1\) for all \(x\in \mathbb{R}\). \end{enumerate}

To prove (1), let \(x\geqslant 0\) then: \begin{equation*} 2+cosh(\sqrt{x}) = 3 + \overunderset{\infty}{n=1}{\sum}\frac{x^n}{(2n)!}\geqslant 3 + \frac{x}{2}+\frac{x^2}{24}. \end{equation*} However, \begin{equation*} 3+\frac{x}{2}+\frac{x^2}{24}\geqslant x \iff \frac{1}{24}(x^2-12x+72)\geqslant 0 \iff \frac{1}{24}((x-6)^2+36)\geqslant 0,s \end{equation*} which concludes the lower bound in the first point. To conclude (1), we note the following for \(x\geqslant0\): \begin{equation*} 3e^{\sqrt{x}}= 3\overunderset{\infty}{n=0}{\sum}\frac{x^{n/2}}{n!}\geqslant 3\overunderset{\infty}{n=0}{\sum}\frac{x^{n}}{(2n)!} \geqslant 2 + \overunderset{\infty}{n=0}{\sum}\frac{x^{n}}{(2n)!}= 2 + cosh(\sqrt{x}). \end{equation*} To prove (2), note that for \(x<0\), \begin{equation*} cosh(\sqrt{x})= \overunderset{\infty}{n=0}{\sum}\frac{x^n}{(2n)!}= \overunderset{\infty}{n=0}{\sum}\frac{(-1)^n \sqrt{-x}^{2n}}{(2n)!}= cos(\sqrt{-x}). \end{equation*} (2) then follows by noting that \(cos(\sqrt{-x}) \in [-1,1]\) for all \(x<0\).

nodes.name: Special function upper bound
nodes.statement: \leavevmode\unskip\nolinebreak\space\textcolor{blue!80!black}{[Lemma 3.3]}\space\ignorespaces Let \(r \in \mathbb{N}\). If \(x_i \geqslant - 3r\) for all \(i \in [r]\), the function \(f \colon \mathbb{R}^r \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) defined in~\eqref{eq:f} satisfies \begin{equation*} f(x_1,\dots,x_r) \leqslant 3^r r \exp\bigg( \displaystyle\sum_{i = 1}^r \sqrt{ x_i + 3r } \bigg) \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:special:function:1

nodes.statement: \begin{equation*} f(x_1,\dots,x_r)= \Bigl(\overunderset{r}{i=1}{\prod}(2+cosh\sqrt{x_i})\Bigr)\overunderset{r}{j=1}{\sum}\frac{x_j}{2+cosh \sqrt{x_j}} \overset{**}{\leqslant}r\Bigl(\overunderset{r}{i=1}{\prod} 3e^{\sqrt{x_i+3r}}\Bigr), \end{equation*} To see (**), we write down upper bounds for all the factors of the LHS of (**). First, for every \(i \in [r]\), such that \(x_i \geqslant 0\), we note that \(cosh(\sqrt{x_i} )\leqslant cosh(\sqrt{x_i+3r})\) (which follows since all the coefficients in the taylor expansion of \(cosh(\sqrt{y}))\) are non-negative and thus \(cosh(\sqrt{y})\) is non-decreasing on the positive reals. In turn, \(2+cosh(\sqrt{x_i+3r}) \leqslant 3e^{\sqrt{x_i+3r}}\) by point 1 of the above remark. We conculde that if \(x_i \geqslant 0\), \(2 + cosh{\sqrt{x_i}} \leqslant 3 e^{\sqrt{x_i+3r}}\). Next, we condiser the indices \(i \in [r]\) such that \(x_i<0\). In this case \begin{equation*} 2+cosh(\sqrt{x_i})= 2 + cos(\sqrt{-x_i}) \leqslant 3 \leqslant 3 e^{\sqrt{x_i+3r}}, \end{equation*} since \(x_i \geqslant -3r\). It remains to show that \(\frac{x_j}{2+cosh(\sqrt{x_j})} \leqslant 1\) for every \(j \in [r]\). If \(x_j\geqslant 0\) this follows directly from point (1) in the above remark. If \(x_j<0\), note that the numerator of the fraction is negative while the denominator is a positive number between 1 and 3 by point(2) of the remark above.

nodes.name: Special function lower bound
nodes.statement: \leavevmode\unskip\nolinebreak\space\textcolor{blue!80!black}{[Lemma 3.3]}\space\ignorespaces Let \(r \in \mathbb{N}\). If there exists an \(i \in [r]\) with \(x_i \leqslant - 3r\), the function \(f \colon \mathbb{R}^r \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) defined in~\eqref{eq:f} satisfies \begin{equation*} f(x_1,\dots,x_r) \leqslant -1 \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:special:function:2

nodes.statement: Let \(i \in [r]\) satisfy \(x_i \leqslant -3r\). Note that if \(x\geqslant 0\), then \(\frac{x}{2+cosh(\sqrt{x})}\leqslant 1\) by point (1) of the above remark. Trivially, we have \(\frac{x}{2+cosh{\sqrt{x}}}<0\leqslant 1\) for \(x<0\) (note that \(2+cosh(\sqrt{x})\geqslant 1\).) Therefore, we have \begin{equation*} \underset{j \in [r], j \neq i}{\sum} \frac{x_j}{2+cosh(\sqrt{x_j})} \leqslant r-1. \end{equation*} On the other hand, we know that \(\frac{x_i}{2+cosh(\sqrt{x_i})} \leqslant \frac{x_i}{3}\) by part (2) in the remark above and therefore, \begin{equation*} \overunderset{r}{j=1}{\sum}\frac{x_j}{2+cosh(\sqrt{x_j})}\leqslant \frac{x_i}{3}+r-1\leqslant -1. \end{equation*} Finally we write \begin{equation*} f(x_1,\dots,x_r) = \Bigl(\overunderset{r}{i=1}{\prod}(2+cosh\sqrt{x_i})\Bigr)\overunderset{r}{j=1}{\sum}\frac{x_j}{2+cosh \sqrt{x_j}} \leqslant -1, \end{equation*} since the sum in the last term is \(\leqslant -1\) while the product is at least \(1\) (each factor in the product is at least 1).

The key idea in the two lemmas above was to find an entire function, \(2 + \cosh\sqrt{x}\), which \((a)\) has a Taylor expansion at \(x = 0\) with non-negative coefficients; \((b)\) is bounded on the negative real axis; and \((c)\) does not grow too quickly on the positive axis. The Phragm\'en--Lindel\"of theorem implies that functions satisfying \((a)\) and \((b)\) must grow at least as fast as \(\exp\big( \Omega(\sqrt{x}) \big)\) on the positive real axis. Thus the bound on the growth of \(f\) given by the lemma is essentially best possible for constructions of this type.

nodes.name: Geometric lemma
nodes.statement: \leavevmode\unskip\nolinebreak\space\textcolor{blue!80!black}{[Lemma 3.1]}\space\ignorespaces Let \(r, n\in\mathbb{N}\). Set \(\beta = 3^{-4r}\) and \(C = 4r^{3/2}\). Let \(U\) and \(U'\) be i.i.d.~random variables taking values in a finite set~\(X\), and let \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r \colon X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^n\) be arbitrary functions. There exists \(\lambda\geqslant-1\) and \(i\in[r]\) such that \begin{equation*} \mathbb{P}\Big( \big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle \geqslant \lambda \, \text{ and } \, \big\langle \sigma_j(U), \sigma_j(U') \big\rangle \geqslant -1 \, \text{ for all } \, j \ne i \Big) \geqslant \beta e^{- C\sqrt{\lambda + 1}}. \end{equation*}
nodes.label: lem:geometric

nodes.statement: For each \(i \in [r]\), define \(Z_i = 3r\big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle\), and let \(E\) be the event that \(Z_i \geqslant -3r\) for every \(i \in [r]\). Consider two cases: First assume \(\mathbb{P}(E) \geqslant \beta\). Note that \begin{equation*} \mathbb{P}(E) = \mathbb{P}\Big( Z_i \geqslant - 3r \, \text{ for all } \, i \in [r] \Big), \end{equation*} so with \(\lambda = -1\), \begin{align*} \beta e^{-C\times 0} &= \beta\\ &\leqslant \mathbb{P}(E)\\ &= \mathbb{P}\Big(3r\big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle \geqslant -3r \text{ for all }i\Big)\\ &= \mathbb{P}\Big( \big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle \geqslant \lambda \, \text{ and } \, \big\langle \sigma_j(U), \sigma_j(U') \big\rangle \geqslant -1 \, \text{ for all } \, j \ne i \Big) \end{align*} hence the claimed inequality holds. Now, assume \(\mathbb{P}(E) \leqslant \beta\) and assume for the sake of a contradiction that for all \(\lambda \geqslant -1\), \begin{align} \mathbb{P}\left(E \cap \left( \bigcup_{i \in [r]} \left\{ \big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle \geqslant \lambda \right\}\right)\right) < \beta r e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda + 1}}. \end{align} Observe that, since \(x \leqslant 2 + \cosh\sqrt{x}\) (\autoref{lem:le-coshsqrt}) and using \autoref{lem:moments} and linearity of expectation, \[ \mathbb{E}\big[ f\big( Z_1,\ldots,Z_r \big) \big] \geqslant 0 \] We hence have \begin{align*} 0 &\leqslant \mathbb{E}\big[ f\big( Z_1,\ldots,Z_r \big) \big]\\ &= \mathbb{E}\big[ f\big( Z_1,\ldots,Z_r \big) \mathbf{1}_E \big] + \mathbb{E}\big[ f\big( Z_1,\ldots,Z_r \big) \mathbf{1}_{E^c} \big]\\ &\leqslant \mathbb{E}\left[ 3^r r \exp\bigg( \displaystyle\sum_{i = 1}^r \sqrt{ Z_i + 3r } \bigg) \mathbf{1}_E \right] + \mathbb{E}\big[-1 \cdot \mathbf{1}_{E^c} \big] \end{align*} where we use \autoref{lem:special:function:1} to bound the case for \(E\), and \autoref{lem:special:function:2} for \(E^c\). It follows that \begin{equation} 1 - \mathbb{P}(E) \leqslant 3^r r \cdot \mathbb{E}\bigg[ \exp\bigg( \sum_{i = 1}^r \sqrt{ Z_i + 3r } \bigg) \mathbf{1}_E \bigg]. \end{equation} Let \(M = \max \big\{ \big\langle \sigma_i(U),\sigma_i(U') \big\rangle : i \in [r] \big\}\). For any constant \(c \leqslant C - 1\), we have \begin{align} \exp(c\sqrt{M+1})\mathrm{id}_E&= \mathrm{id}_E \Bigl(e^{c\sqrt{1-1}}+ \int_{-1}^M \frac{ce^{c\sqrt{\lambda+1}}}{2\sqrt{\lambda+1}} d\lambda\Bigr)\\ &= \mathrm{id}_E+ \int_{-1}^{\infty} \mathrm{id}_{E,\{M\geqslant \lambda\}}\frac{ce^{c\sqrt{\lambda+1}}}{2\sqrt{\lambda+1}} d\lambda. \end{align} Given any \(c \leqslant C-1\) we take the expected value of both sides of the previous equation and apply Tonelli's theorem to obtain: \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\Big[ \exp\big( c \sqrt{M + 1} \big) \mathbf{1}_E \Big] & \\ & \leqslant \, \mathbb{P}(E) + \int_{-1}^\infty \mathbb{P}\Big( \big\{ M \geqslant \lambda \big\} \cap E \Big) \cdot \frac{c}{2\sqrt{\lambda + 1}} \cdot e^{c \sqrt{\lambda + 1}} \,\mathrm{d}\lambda\\ & \leqslant \, \beta + \int_{-1}^\infty \frac{\beta r c}{2\sqrt{\lambda + 1}} \cdot e^{- C\sqrt{\lambda + 1}+c\sqrt{\lambda+1}} \,\mathrm{d}\lambda\\ & \leqslant \, \beta + \beta r \int_{-1}^\infty \frac{c}{2\sqrt{\lambda + 1}} \cdot e^{- \sqrt{\lambda + 1}} \,\mathrm{d}\lambda\\ & \leqslant \, \beta (cr + 1), \end{align*} where in the second inequality we used (\autoref{eq:max:big:and:E:no}) and \(\mathbb{P}(E) \leqslant \beta\); in the third we used \(c \leqslant C - 1\); and in the last inequality we used the fact that \(\int_0^\infty \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} e^{-\sqrt{x}} \, \mathrm{d}x = 1\). Note that the second and third inequalities rely on the non-negativity of the integrand. In particular, applying this with \(c = \sqrt{3}r^{3/2}\), and recalling that \(C = 4r^{3/2} \geqslant c + 1\) and \(\beta = 3^{-4r}\), it follows that \begin{align} 1 - \mathbb{P}(E) &\leqslant 3^r r \cdot \mathbb{E}\bigg[ \exp\bigg( \sum_{i = 1}^r \sqrt{ Z_i + 3r } \bigg) \mathbf{1}_E \bigg]\\ &\leqslant 3^r r \cdot \mathbb{E}\bigg[ \ex

nodes.name: Key lemma
nodes.statement: \leavevmode\unskip\nolinebreak\space\textcolor{blue!80!black}{[Lemma 2.2]}\space\ignorespaces Let \(r, n\in\mathbb{N}\). Set \(\beta = 3^{-4r}\) and \(C = 4r^{3/2}\). Let \(\chi\) be an \(r\)-colouring of \(E(K_n)\), let \(X,Y_1,\ldots,Y_r \subset V(K_n)\) be non-empty sets of vertices, and let \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r > 0\). There exists a vertex \(x \in X\), a colour \(\ell \in [r]\), sets \(X' \subset X\) and \(Y'_1,\ldots,Y'_r\,\) with \(Y'_i \subset N_i(x) \cap Y_i\,\) for each \(i \in [r]\), and \(\lambda \geqslant -1\), such that \begin{equation} \beta e^{- C \sqrt{\lambda + 1}} |X| \leqslant |X'| \qquad \text{and} \qquad p_\ell(X,Y_\ell) + \lambda \alpha_\ell \leqslant p_\ell( X', Y'_\ell ) , \end{equation} and moreover \begin{equation} |Y'_i| = p_i(X,Y_i) |Y_i| \qquad \text{and} \qquad p_i(X,Y_i) - \alpha_i \leqslant p_i( X', Y'_i ) \end{equation} for every \(i \in [r]\).
nodes.label: lem:key-lemma

nodes.statement: For each colour \(i \in [r]\), define a function \(\sigma_i \colon X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{\cup_i Y_i}\) as follows: for each \(x \in X\), choose a set \(N'_i(x) \subset N_i(x) \cap Y_i\) of size exactly \(p_i|Y_i|\), where \(p_i = p_i(X,Y_i)\), and set \begin{equation*} \sigma_i(x) = \frac{\mathrm{id}_{N'_i(x)} - p_i\mathrm{id}_{Y_i}}{\sqrt{\alpha_ip_i|Y_i|}}, \end{equation*} where \(\mathrm{id}_S \in \{0,1\}^{\cup_i Y_i}\) denotes the indicator function of the set \(S\). Note that, for any \(x,y\in X\), \begin{equation*} \lambda \leqslant \big\langle \sigma_i(x),\sigma_i(y) \big\rangle \quad \Leftrightarrow \quad \big( p_i + \lambda\alpha_i \big) p_i |Y_i| \leqslant |N'_i(x) \cap N'_i(y)|. \end{equation*} Indeed, for every \(x,y\in X\), we have \begin{multline} \begin{aligned} \alpha_ip_i|Y_i| \langle \sigma_i(x),\sigma_i(y) \rangle &= \langle \mathrm{id}_{N'_i(x)}- p_i\mathrm{id}_{Y_i},\mathrm{id}_{N'_i(y)}- p_i\mathrm{id}_{Y_i}\rangle\\ &= \Bigl(\big\langle \mathrm{id}_{N'_i(x)},\mathrm{id}_{N'_i(y)}\big\rangle +p_i^2\langle \mathrm{id}_{Y_i}, \mathrm{id}_{Y_i}\rangle - p_i \langle \mathrm{id}_{N'_i(x)},\mathrm{id}_{Y_i}\rangle- p_i \langle \mathrm{id}_{N'_i(y)},\mathrm{id}_{Y_i}\rangle\Bigr)\\ &= \Bigl(|N'_i(x) \cap N'_i(y)|-p_i^2|Y_i| \Bigr), \end{aligned} \end{multline} Where the last ineqaulity follows since \(|N'_i(x)|= N'_i(y)|= p_i|Y_i|\) and both sets are subsets of \(Y_i\). Now, by \autoref{lem:geometric}, there exists \(\lambda \geqslant -1\) and colour \(\ell \in [r]\) such that \begin{equation} \beta e^{- C\sqrt{\lambda + 1}} \leqslant \mathbb{P}\Big( \lambda \leqslant \big\langle \sigma_\ell(U),\sigma_\ell(U') \big\rangle \, \text{ and } \, -1 \leqslant \big\langle \sigma_i(U), \sigma_i(U') \big\rangle \, \text{ for all } \, i \ne \ell \Big) . \end{equation} where \(U\), \(U'\) are independent random variables distributed uniformly in the set~\(X\). We claim that there exists a vertex \(x \in X\) and a set \(X' \subset X\) such that, \begin{equation*} \beta e^{- C \sqrt{\lambda + 1}} |X| \leqslant |X'| \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} \big( p_\ell + \lambda\alpha_\ell \big) p_\ell |Y_\ell | \leqslant |N'_\ell(x) \cap N'_\ell(y)| \end{equation*} for every \(y \in X'\), and \begin{equation*} \big( p_i - \alpha_i \big) p_i |Y_i| \leqslant |N'_i(x) \cap N'_i(y)| \end{equation*} for every \(y \in X'\) and \(i \in [r]\). To see this, we let \begin{equation*} P= \Biggl\{(x,x'): x,x' \in X , \lambda \leqslant \big\langle \sigma_\ell(x),\sigma_\ell(x') \big\rangle \, \text{ and } \, -1 \leqslant \big\langle \sigma_i(x), \sigma_i(x') \big\rangle \, \text{ for all } \, i \ne \ell \Biggr\}. \end{equation*} Since \(U\) and \(U'\) are independent and uniformly distributed over \(x\), Equation \autoref{eq: geometric-app} implies that \begin{equation} |P|\geqslant \beta e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda + 1}}|X|^2. \end{equation} However, by averaging, there must then exist a vertex \(x \in X\) such that: \begin{equation} |X'|:=\bigl|\{y: (x,y) \in P \} \bigr| \geqslant \frac{\beta e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda+1}}|X|^2}{|X|}\geqslant \beta e^{-C\sqrt{\lambda+1}}|X|. \end{equation} We can them simply pick this \(X'\) to be the desired subset. Setting \(Y'_i = N'_i(x)\) for each \(i \in [r]\), it follows that \begin{multline} \begin{aligned} p_\ell(X,Y_\ell) + \lambda \alpha_\ell &= \frac{ \big( p_\ell + \lambda\alpha_\ell \big) p_\ell |Y_\ell |}{p_\ell |Y_\ell|}\\ &= \frac{ \big( p_\ell + \lambda\alpha_\ell \big) p_\ell |Y_\ell |}{| N'_\ell (x)|}\\ &= \min\bigg\{ \frac{ \big( p_\ell + \lambda\alpha_\ell \big) p_\ell |Y_\ell |}{| N'_\ell (x)|} : x' \in X' \bigg\}\\ &\leqslant \min\bigg\{ \frac{|N'_\ell(x') \cap N'_\ell (x)|}{| N'_\ell (x)|} : x' \in X' \bigg\}\\ &= \min\bigg\{ \frac{|N_\ell(x') \cap N'_\ell (x)|}{| N'_\ell (x)|} : x' \in X' \bigg\}\\ &= p_\ell\big( X', N'_\ell (x) \big) = p_\ell\big( X', Y'_\ell \big) \\ \end{aligned} \end{multline} and \begin{equation*} p_i(X,Y_i) - \alpha_i \leqslant \qquad p_i\big( X', Y'_i \big) \end{equatio

nodes.name: Lower bound for \(p_i\) during algorithm
nodes.statement: \leavevmode\unskip\nolinebreak\space\textcolor{blue!80!black}{[Lemma 4.1]}\space\ignorespaces For each \(i \in [r]\) and \(s \in \mathbb{N}\), \begin{equation} p_i(s) - p_0 + \delta \, \geqslant \, \delta \cdot \bigg( 1 - \frac{1}{t} \bigg)^{t} \prod_{j \in \mathcal{B}_i(s)} \bigg( 1 + \frac{\lambda(j)}{t} \bigg). \end{equation}
nodes.label: lem:pi:lower:bound

nodes.statement: Note first that if \(Y_i(s+1) = Y_i(s)\), then \(p_i(s+1) \geqslant p_i(s)\), since the minimum degree does not decrease when we take a subset of \(X(s)\). When we perform a colour step in colour \(i\), we have \(p_i(s+1) \geqslant p_i(s) - \alpha_i(s)\), by \autoref{lem:key-lemma}, and hence \begin{equation*} p_i(s+1) - p_0 + \delta \geqslant \bigg( 1 - \frac{1}{t} \bigg) \big( p_i(s) - p_0 + \delta \big), \end{equation*} by our choice of \(\alpha_i(s)\). Similarly, when we perform a density-boost step in colour \(i\) we have \(p_i(s+1) \geqslant p_i(s) + \lambda(s) \alpha_i(s)\), by \autoref{lem:key-lemma}, and hence \begin{equation*} p_i(s+1) - p_0 + \delta \geqslant \bigg( 1 + \frac{\lambda(s)}{t} \bigg) \big( p_i(s) - p_0 + \delta \big). \end{equation*} Recalling that there are at most \(t\) colour steps in colour \(i\), and that \(p_i(0) \geqslant p_0\), by the definition~\eqref{def:p0} of \(p_0\), the claimed bound follows.

nodes.name: Minimum bounds on \(p_i\) and \(\alpha_i\)
nodes.statement: \leavevmode\unskip\nolinebreak\space\textcolor{blue!80!black}{[Lemma 4.2]}\space\ignorespaces If \(t \geqslant 2\), then \begin{equation*} p_i(s) \, \geqslant \, p_0 - \frac{3\delta}{4} \end{equation*} for every \(i \in [r]\) and \(s \in \mathbb{N}\).
nodes.label: lem:pi:minp

nodes.statement: Bound follows immediately from~\eqref{eq:pi:lower:bound} and the definition of \(\alpha_i(s)\).

nodes.name: Minimum bounds on \(p_i\) and \(\alpha_i\)
nodes.statement: \leavevmode\unskip\nolinebreak\space\textcolor{blue!80!black}{[Lemma 4.2]}\space\ignorespaces If \(t \geqslant 2\), then \begin{equation*} \alpha_i(s) \, \geqslant \, \frac{\delta}{4t} \end{equation*} for every \(i \in [r]\) and \(s \in \mathbb{N}\).
nodes.label: lem:pi:mina

nodes.statement: Bound follows immediately from~\eqref{eq:pi:lower:bound} and the definition of \(\alpha_i(s)\).

nodes.name: Upper bound on density-boost steps
nodes.statement: \leavevmode\unskip\nolinebreak\space\textcolor{blue!80!black}{[Lemma 4.3]}\space\ignorespaces If \(t \geqslant \lambda_0\) and \(\delta \leqslant 1/4\), then \begin{equation*} |\mathcal{B}_i(s)| \leqslant \frac{4 \log(1/\delta)}{\lambda_0} \cdot t \end{equation*} for every \(i \in [r]\) and \(s \in \mathbb{N}\).
nodes.label: lem:Bi:max

nodes.statement: Since \(\lambda(j) > \lambda_0\) for every \(j \in \mathcal{B}_i(s)\), and \(p_i(s) \leqslant 1\), it follows from~\eqref{eq:pi:lower:bound} that \begin{equation*} \frac{\delta}{4} \bigg( 1 + \frac{\lambda_0}{t} \bigg)^{|\mathcal{B}_i(s)|} \leqslant 1 + \delta. \end{equation*} Since \(t \geqslant \lambda_0\) and \(\delta \leqslant 1/4\), the claimed bound follows.

nodes.name: Lower bound for \(Y_i\) set sizes
nodes.statement: \leavevmode\unskip\nolinebreak\space\textcolor{blue!80!black}{[Lemma 4.4]}\space\ignorespaces If \(t \geqslant 2\), then \begin{equation*} |Y_i(s)| \geqslant \bigg( p_0 - \frac{3\delta}{4} \bigg)^{t + |\mathcal{B}_i(s)|} |Y_i(0)| \end{equation*} for every \(i \in [r]\) and \(s \in \mathbb{N}\).
nodes.label: lem:Y:lower:bound

nodes.statement: Note that \(Y_i(j+1) \ne Y_i(j)\) for at most \(t + |\mathcal{B}_i(s)|\) of the first \(s\) steps, and for those steps we have \begin{equation*} |Y_i(j+1)| = p_i(j) |Y_i(j)| \geqslant \bigg( p_0 - \frac{3\delta}{4} \bigg) |Y_i(j)|, \end{equation*} by~\eqref{eq:key:alli} and \autoref{lem:pi:mina}.

nodes.name: Lower bound for reservoir X size
nodes.statement: \leavevmode\unskip\nolinebreak\space\textcolor{blue!80!black}{[Lemma 4.5]}\space\ignorespaces For each \(s \in \mathbb{N}\), \begin{equation} |X(s)| \geqslant \varepsilon^{rt + |\mathcal{B}(s)|} \exp\bigg( - C \sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}(s)} \sqrt{\lambda(j)+1}\,\, \bigg) |X(0)| - rt. \end{equation}
nodes.label: lem:X:lower:bound

nodes.statement: If \(\lambda(j) \leqslant \lambda_0\), then by~\eqref{eq:key:ell} and Step~2 of the algorithm we have \begin{equation*} |X(j+1)| \geqslant \frac{\beta e^{- C \sqrt{\lambda_0 + 1}}}{r} \cdot |X(j)| - 1 = \varepsilon |X(j)| - 1. \end{equation*} On the other hand, if \(\lambda(j) > \lambda_0\), then \(j \in \mathcal{B}(s)\), and we have \begin{equation*} |X(j+1)| \geqslant \beta e^{- C \sqrt{\lambda(j) + 1}} |X(j)|, \end{equation*} by~\eqref{eq:key:ell} and Step~3 of the algorithm. Since there are at most \(rt\) colour steps, and \(\beta \geqslant \varepsilon\), the claimed bound follows.

nodes.name: Sum of \(\lambda\) parameters bound
nodes.statement: \leavevmode\unskip\nolinebreak\space\textcolor{blue!80!black}{[Lemma 4.6]}\space\ignorespaces If \(t \geqslant \lambda_0 / \delta > 0\) and \(\delta \leqslant 1/4\), then \begin{equation*} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}(s)} \sqrt{\lambda(j)} \leqslant \frac{7r \log(1/\delta)}{\sqrt{\lambda_0}} \cdot t \end{equation*} for every \(s \in \mathbb{N}\).
nodes.label: lem:sum:of:lambdas

nodes.statement: Observe first that, by \autoref{lem:pi:lower:bound}, we have \begin{equation} \frac{\delta}{4} \prod_{j \in \mathcal{B}_i(s)} \bigg( 1 + \frac{\lambda(j)}{t} \bigg) \leqslant 1 + \delta \end{equation} for each \(i \in [r]\). Note also that \(\lambda_0 \leqslant \lambda(j) \leqslant 5t/\delta\) for every \(j \in \mathcal{B}(s)\), where the lower bound holds by the definition of \(\mathcal{B}(s)\), and the upper bound by~\eqref{eq:B:condition} and since \(\delta \leqslant 1/4\). Now, since \(\log(1+x) \geqslant \min\{ x/2,1\}\) for all \(x > 0\), it follows that \begin{equation} \frac{ \sqrt{\lambda(j)} }{\log(1 + \lambda(j)/t) } \leqslant \max\bigg\{ \frac{ 2t }{ \sqrt{\lambda_0} }, \, \sqrt{ \frac{5t}{\delta}} \bigg\} \leqslant \frac{ 3t }{ \sqrt{\lambda_0} }, \end{equation} where in the second inequality we used our assumption that \(t \geqslant \lambda_0 / \delta\). It now follows that \begin{equation*} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}_i(s)} \sqrt{\lambda(j)} \leqslant \frac{ 3t }{ \sqrt{\lambda_0} } \sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}_i(s)} \log \bigg( 1 + \frac{\lambda(j)}{t} \bigg) \leqslant \frac{7 \log(1/\delta)}{\sqrt{\lambda_0}} \cdot t, \end{equation*} where the first inequality holds by~\eqref{eq:not:convexity}, and the second follows from~\eqref{eq:B:condition}, since \(\delta \leqslant 1/4\). Summing over \(i \in [r]\), we obtain the claimed bound.

nodes.name: Book theorem
nodes.statement: \leavevmode\unskip\nolinebreak\space\textcolor{blue!80!black}{[Theorem 2.1]}\space\ignorespaces Let \(\chi\) be an \(r\)-colouring of \(E(K_n)\), and let \(X,Y_1,\ldots,Y_r \subset V(K_n)\). For every \(p > 0\) and \(\mu \geqslant 2^{10} r^3\), and every \(t,m \in \mathbb{N}\) with \(t \geqslant \mu^5 / p\), the following holds. If \begin{equation*} |N_i(x) \cap Y_i| \geqslant p|Y_i| \end{equation*} for every \(x \in X\) and \(i \in [r]\), and moreover \begin{equation*} |X| \geqslant \bigg( \frac{\mu^2}{p} \bigg)^{\mu r t} \qquad \text{and} \qquad |Y_i| \geqslant \bigg( \frac{e^{2^{13} r^3 / \mu^2}}{p} \bigg)^t \, m, \end{equation*} then \(\chi\) contains a monochromatic \((t,m)\)-book.
nodes.label: thm:book

nodes.statement: Recall that we are given an \(r\)-colouring \(\chi\) of \(E(K_n)\) and a collection of sets \(X,Y_1,\ldots,Y_r \subset V(K_n)\) with \begin{equation} |X| \geqslant \bigg( \frac{\mu^2}{p} \bigg)^{\mu r t} \qquad \text{and} \qquad |Y_i| \geqslant \bigg( \frac{e^{2^{13} r^3 / \mu^2}}{p} \bigg)^t \, m \end{equation} for each \(i \in [r]\), for some \(p > 0\), \(\mu \geqslant 2^{10} r^3\) and \(t,m \in \mathbb{N}\) with \(t \geqslant \mu^5 / p\), and moreover \begin{equation} |N_i(x) \cap Y_i| \geqslant p|Y_i| \end{equation} for every \(x \in X\) and \(i \in [r]\). We will run the multicolour book algorithm with \begin{equation*} \delta = \frac{p}{\mu^2} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \lambda_0 = \bigg( \frac{\mu \log(1/\delta)}{8C} \bigg)^2, \end{equation*} where \(C = 4r^{3/2}\) (as before), and show that it ends with \begin{equation*} \max \big\{ |T_i(s)| : i \in [r] \big\} = t \qquad \text{and} \qquad \min\big\{ |Y_i(s)| : i \in [r] \big\} \geqslant m, \end{equation*} and therefore produces a monochromatic \((t,m)\)-book. To do so, we just need to bound the sizes of the sets \(X(s)\) and \(Y_i(s)\) from below. Observe that \(t \geqslant \lambda_0\) and \(\delta \leqslant 1/4\), and therefore, by \autoref{lem:Bi:max}, that \begin{equation} |\mathcal{B}_i(s)| \, \leqslant \, \frac{4 \log(1/\delta)}{\lambda_0} \cdot t \, = \, \frac{2^{12} r^3}{\mu^2 \log(1/\delta)} \cdot t \, \leqslant \, t \end{equation} for every \(i \in [r]\) and \(s \in \mathbb{N}\). Since \(p_0 \geqslant p\), by~\eqref{eq:book:thm:min:degree} and the definition of \(p_0\), it follows that \begin{equation*} |Y_i(s)| \, \geqslant \, \bigg( p - \frac{3\delta}{4} \bigg)^{t + |\mathcal{B}_i(s)|} |Y_i| \, \geqslant \, e^{-2\delta t / p} \, p^{|\mathcal{B}_i(s)|} \, \big( e^{2^{13} r^3 / \mu^2} \big)^t \, m, \end{equation*} where the first inequality holds by \autoref{lem:Y:lower:bound}, and the second by~\eqref{eq:book:thm:conditions} and~\eqref{eq:Bi:final:bound}. Noting that \(p^{|\mathcal{B}_i(s)|} \geqslant e^{-2^{12} r^3 t / \mu^2}\), by~\eqref{eq:Bi:final:bound}, and that \(\delta / p = 1/\mu^2\), it follows that \begin{equation*} |Y_i(s)| \, \geqslant \, e^{-2 t / \mu^2} \big( e^{2^{12} r^3 / \mu^2} \big)^t \, m \, \geqslant \, m, \end{equation*} as claimed. To bound \(|X(s)|\), recall~\eqref{eq:X:lower:bound} and observe that \begin{equation*} \varepsilon^{rt + |\mathcal{B}(s)|} \geqslant \bigg( \frac{\beta}{r} \cdot e^{- C \sqrt{\lambda_0 + 1}} \bigg)^{2rt} \geqslant \big( e^{- 4C \sqrt{\lambda_0}} \big)^{rt} = \delta^{\mu r t/2} = \bigg( \frac{\mu^2}{p} \bigg)^{-\mu r t / 2}, \end{equation*} where the first step holds because \(\varepsilon = (\beta / r) e^{- C \sqrt{\lambda_0 + 1}}\) and \(|\mathcal{B}(s)| \leqslant rt\), by~\eqref{eq:Bi:final:bound}, and the second step holds because \(\beta = 3^{-4r}\) and \(\lambda_0 \geqslant 2^{10} r^3\). Moreover, we have \begin{equation*} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{B}(s)} \sqrt{\lambda(j)+1} \leqslant \frac{8r \log(1/\delta)}{\sqrt{\lambda_0}} \cdot t = \frac{2^6Crt}{\mu}, \end{equation*} by \autoref{lem:sum:of:lambdas} and our choice of \(\lambda_0\), and therefore \begin{equation*} |X(s)| \geqslant \bigg( \frac{\mu^2}{p} \bigg)^{\mu r t / 2} \exp\bigg( - \frac{2^6C^2rt}{\mu} \bigg) - rt > 0, \end{equation*} for every \(s \in \mathbb{N}\), by \autoref{lem:X:lower:bound} and since \(\mu \geqslant 2^{10} r^3\) and \(C = 4r^{3/2}\). It follows that the algorithm produces a monochromatic \((t,m)\)-book, as claimed.

nodes.name: Single Erdős-Szekeres step
nodes.statement: \leavevmode\unskip\nolinebreak\space\textcolor{blue!80!black}{[Lemma 5.2]}\space\ignorespaces Given \(n,r \in \mathbb{N}\) and \(\varepsilon > 0\), and an \(r\)-colouring of \(E(K_n)\), the following holds. There exist disjoint sets of vertices \(S_1,\dots,S_r\) and \(W\) such that, for every \(i \in [r]\), \begin{equation*} |W| \geqslant \bigg( \frac{1+\varepsilon}{r} \bigg)^{\sum_{j = 1}^r |S_j|} n \qquad \text{and} \qquad |N_i(w) \cap W| \geqslant \bigg( \frac{1}{r} - \varepsilon \bigg) |W| - 1 \end{equation*} for every \(w \in W\), and \((S_i,W)\) is a monochromatic book in colour~\(i\).
nodes.section: 6 Deducing the Bound on the Ramsey Number
nodes.label: lem:ESz:steps

nodes.statement: We use induction on~\(n\). Note that if \(n \leqslant r\) or \(r = 1\), then the sets \(S_1 = \cdots = S_r = \emptyset\) and \(W = V(K_n)\) have the required properties. We may therefore assume that \(n > r \geqslant 2\), and that there exists a vertex \(x \in V(K_n)\) and a colour \(\ell \in [r]\) such that \begin{equation*} |N_\ell(x)| < \bigg( \frac{1}{r} - \varepsilon \bigg) n - 1, \end{equation*} and hence there exists a different colour \(j \ne \ell\) such that \begin{equation*} |N_j(x)| \geqslant \frac{1}{r-1} \bigg( n - \bigg( \frac{1}{r} - \varepsilon \bigg) n \bigg) \geqslant \bigg( \frac{1 + \varepsilon}{r} \bigg) n. \end{equation*} Applying the induction hypothesis to the colouring induced by the set \(N_j(x)\), we obtain sets \(S'_1,\ldots,S'_r\) and \(W'\) satisfying the conclusion of the lemma with \(n\) replaced by \(|N_j(x)|\). Setting \begin{equation*} W = W', \qquad S_j = S'_j \cup \{x\} \qquad \text{and} \qquad S_i = S'_i \qquad \text{for each } \, i \ne j, \end{equation*} we see that \(W\) satisfies the minimum degree condition (by the induction hypothesis), and \begin{equation*} |W| \geqslant \bigg( \frac{1+\varepsilon}{r} \bigg)^{\sum_{i = 1}^r |S'_i|}|N_j(x)| \geqslant \bigg( \frac{1+\varepsilon}{r} \bigg)^{\sum_{i=1}^r |S_i|}n. \end{equation*} Since \((S_i,W)\) is a monochromatic book in colour~\(i\) for each \(i \in [r]\), it follows that \(S_1,\dots,S_r\) and \(W\) are sets with the claimed properties.
nodes.section: 6 Deducing the Bound on the Ramsey Number

nodes.name: Many Erdős-Szekeres steps bound
nodes.statement: \leavevmode\unskip\nolinebreak\space\textcolor{blue!80!black}{[Lemma 5.3]}\space\ignorespaces Let \(k,r \geqslant 2\) and \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\). We have \begin{equation*} R_r\big( k - s_1, \ldots, k - s_r \big) \leqslant e^{-\varepsilon^3 k / 2} \bigg( \frac{1+\varepsilon}{r} \bigg)^s r^{rk} \end{equation*} for every \(s_1,\ldots,s_r \in [k]\) with \(s = s_1 + \cdots + s_r \geqslant \varepsilon^2 k\).
nodes.section: 6 Deducing the Bound on the Ramsey Number
nodes.label: lem:many:ESz:steps

nodes.statement: By the Erd\H{o}s--Szekeres bound, we have \begin{equation*} R_r\big( k - s_1, \ldots, k - s_r \big) \leqslant r^{rk - s}. \end{equation*} The claimed bound follows, since \(( 1 + \varepsilon )^{\varepsilon^2 k} \geqslant e^{\varepsilon^3 k/2}\) for every \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\).
nodes.section: 6 Deducing the Bound on the Ramsey Number

nodes.name: Quantitative main theorem
nodes.statement: \leavevmode\unskip\nolinebreak\space\textcolor{blue!80!black}{[Theorem 5.1]}\space\ignorespaces Let \(r \geqslant 2\), and set \(\delta = 2^{-160} r^{-12}\). Then \begin{equation*} R_r(k) \leqslant e^{-\delta k} r^{rk} \end{equation*} for every \(k \in \mathbb{N}\) with \(k \geqslant 2^{160} r^{16}\).
nodes.section: 6 Deducing the Bound on the Ramsey Number
nodes.label: thm:Ramsey:multicolour:quant

nodes.statement: Given \(r \geqslant 2\), set \(\delta = 2^{-160} r^{-12}\), let \(k \geqslant 2^{160} r^{16}\) and \(n \geqslant e^{-\delta k} r^{rk}\), and let \(\chi\) be an arbitrary \(r\)-colouring of \(E(K_n)\). Set \(\varepsilon = 2^{-50} r^{-4}\), and let \(S_1,\ldots,S_r\) and \(W\) be the sets given by \autoref{lem:ESz:steps}. Suppose first that \(|S_1| + \cdots + |S_r| \geqslant \varepsilon^2 k\), and observe that, by \autoref{lem:many:ESz:steps} and our lower bounds on \(n\) and \(|W|\), we have \begin{equation*} |W| \geqslant \bigg( \frac{1+\varepsilon}{r} \bigg)^{\sum_{j = 1}^r |S_j|} e^{-\delta k} r^{rk} \geqslant R_r\big( k - |S_1|, \ldots, k - |S_r| \big). \end{equation*} Since \((S_i,W)\) is a monochromatic book in colour~\(i\) for each \(i \in [r]\), it follows that there exists a monochromatic copy of \(K_k\) in \(\chi\), as required. We may therefore assume from now on that \(|S_1| + \cdots + |S_r| \leqslant \varepsilon^2 k\). In this case we set \(X = Y_1 = \cdots = Y_r = W\), and apply \autoref{thm:book} to the colouring restricted to \(W\) with \begin{equation*} p = \frac{1}{r} - 2\varepsilon, \qquad \mu = 2^{30} r^3, \qquad t = 2^{-40} r^{-3} k \qquad \text{and} \qquad m = R\big( k, \ldots, k, k - t \big). \end{equation*} In order to apply \autoref{thm:book}, we need to check that \(t \geqslant \mu^5/p\), and that \begin{equation*} |X| \geqslant \bigg( \frac{\mu^2}{p} \bigg)^{\mu r t} \qquad \text{and} \qquad |Y_i| \geqslant \bigg( \frac{e^{2^{13} r^3 / \mu^2}}{p} \bigg)^t \, m. \end{equation*} The first two of these inequalities are both easy: the first holds because \(k \geqslant 2^{160} r^{16}\), and for the second note that since \(n \geqslant r^{rk/2}\) and \(\sum_{j = 1}^r |S_j| \leqslant rk/4\), we have \begin{equation*} |X| \geqslant \bigg( \frac{1+\varepsilon}{r} \bigg)^{rk/4} r^{rk/2} \geqslant r^{rk/4} \geqslant \big( 2^{61} r^7 \big)^{2^{-10} r k} \geqslant \bigg( \frac{\mu^2}{p} \bigg)^{\mu r t}, \end{equation*} as required. The third inequality is more delicate: observe first that \begin{equation*} R\big( k, \ldots, k, k-t \big) \leqslant \binom{rk-t}{k,\dots,k,k-t} \leqslant e^{-(r-1)t^2/3rk} r^{rk-t} \leqslant e^{-t^2/6k} r^{rk-t}. \end{equation*} and therefore, since \(\delta \leqslant 2^{-10} t^2/k^2\) and \(p = 1/r - 2\varepsilon \geqslant e^{-3\varepsilon r} / r\), we have \begin{equation*} n \geqslant e^{-\delta k} r^{rk} \geqslant r^t e^{t^2/8k} \cdot R\big( k, \ldots, k, k-t \big) \geqslant \frac{m}{p^t} \cdot \exp\bigg( \frac{t^2}{8k} - 3\varepsilon r t \bigg). \end{equation*} Moreover, by our choice of \(t\) and \(\mu\), we have \begin{equation*} \frac{t}{8k} = \frac{1}{2^{43} r^3} \geqslant \frac{1}{2^{47}r^3} + \frac{1}{2^{48}r^3} = \frac{2^{13} r^3}{\mu^2} + 4\varepsilon r. \end{equation*} Finally, since \(\sum_{j = 1}^r |S_j| \leqslant \varepsilon^2 k \leqslant \varepsilon t\), it follows that \begin{equation*} |Y_i| = |W| \geqslant \bigg( \frac{1+\varepsilon}{r} \bigg)^{\varepsilon t} n \geqslant \frac{m}{p^t} \cdot \exp\bigg( \frac{t^2}{8k} - 4\varepsilon r t \bigg) \geqslant \bigg( \frac{e^{2^{13} r^3 / \mu^2}}{p} \bigg)^t \, m, \end{equation*} as claimed. Thus \(\chi\) contains a monochromatic \((t,m)\)-book, and hence, by our choice of \(m\), \(\chi\) contains a monochromatic copy of \(K_k\), as required.
nodes.section: 6 Deducing the Bound on the Ramsey Number
